sectionToMerge.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About Lu-177 PSMA Therapy (Pluvicto) for Prostate Cancer
sectionToMerge.intro: Lu-177 PSMA therapy, known by the brand name Pluvicto, is a targeted radioligand treatment used for certain types of advanced prostate cancer. These FAQs explain how it works, who may qualify, and what international patients should know.

items.a: Lu-177 PSMA therapy is a targeted radioligand treatment that delivers radiation directly to prostate cancer cells. It combines a molecule that binds to prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) with the radioactive isotope Lutetium-177. Once attached to PSMA-positive cancer cells, it releases radiation that damages them while limiting harm to nearby healthy tissue. Marketed as Pluvicto, it is used for selected patients with advanced prostate cancer after specialist review.

items.q: How does Lu-177 PSMA therapy work?
items.a: Lu-177 PSMA therapy works by seeking out prostate cancer cells that carry the PSMA protein on their surface. The therapy is given by intravenous infusion, after which the PSMA-targeting molecule attaches to cancer cells throughout the body. The attached Lutetium-177 then emits short-range radiation that damages the DNA of those cells. Because it targets PSMA specifically, it can reach cancer that has spread while sparing much surrounding healthy tissue.

items.q: What is PSMA and why does it matter for this treatment?
items.a: PSMA, or prostate-specific membrane antigen, is a protein found in high amounts on the surface of most prostate cancer cells. It matters because Lu-177 PSMA therapy uses PSMA as a target to deliver radiation precisely where cancer cells are located. Before treatment, a PSMA PET scan is usually performed to confirm that the cancer is PSMA-positive. Patients whose tumors do not express PSMA may not benefit from this therapy.

items.q: Is Lu-177 PSMA therapy the same as chemotherapy?
items.a: No, Lu-177 PSMA therapy is not chemotherapy; it is a form of targeted radioligand therapy. Chemotherapy uses drugs that circulate through the body to kill rapidly dividing cells, while Lu-177 PSMA delivers radiation directly to PSMA-positive prostate cancer cells. The two treatments work by different mechanisms and have different side-effect profiles. In some care plans they may be used at different stages, as decided by the treating oncology team.

items.q: Who is eligible for Lu-177 PSMA therapy?
items.a: Lu-177 PSMA therapy may be considered for adults with PSMA-positive metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer who have already received certain hormonal and chemotherapy treatments. Eligibility depends on cancer type, stage, PSMA PET scan results, previous therapies, kidney and bone marrow function, and overall health. A specialist confirms suitability after reviewing scans and reports. Final decisions about whether this treatment is appropriate should always be made by the treating medical team.

items.q: How is Lu-177 PSMA therapy given?
items.a: Lu-177 PSMA therapy is given as an intravenous infusion, usually every six weeks for up to six cycles. Before each cycle, doctors typically check blood counts, kidney function, and overall condition. After the infusion, patients receive guidance on radiation safety precautions for a short period, since small amounts of radioactivity remain in the body. The exact number of cycles and schedule depends on how the cancer responds and the specialist's assessment.

items.q: What are the side effects of Lu-177 PSMA therapy?
items.a: Common side effects of Lu-177 PSMA therapy may include tiredness, dry mouth, nausea, reduced appetite, and lower blood cell counts. Because the treatment involves radiation, kidney function and bone marrow are monitored closely during the course. Most side effects are manageable, but some can be serious and require medical attention. Side effects vary between patients, and any symptoms should be discussed promptly with the treating oncology team for appropriate care.

items.q: How effective is Lu-177 PSMA therapy?
items.a: Lu-177 PSMA therapy has shown benefit in selected patients with advanced PSMA-positive prostate cancer, including improvements in disease control and quality of life in clinical studies. However, responses vary from person to person, and the therapy is not a cure. Its effectiveness depends on cancer stage, PSMA expression, previous treatments, and overall health. Realistic expectations and treatment goals should be discussed carefully with the treating medical team before starting.

items.q: How much does Lu-177 PSMA therapy cost?
items.a: The cost of Lu-177 PSMA therapy varies widely by country, hospital, and number of cycles required. Estimated costs may range from a few thousand dollars per cycle to significantly more, but figures are not fixed. Final cost depends on the hospital, diagnosis, stage, scans such as PSMA PET, supportive care, complications, and length of stay. A detailed estimate should be obtained from the treating center after medical review.

items.q: Is Lu-177 PSMA therapy available in India?
items.a: Lu-177 PSMA therapy is available at selected specialized cancer and nuclear medicine centers in India. Availability depends on the hospital's radioligand therapy facilities, isotope supply, and specialist teams. Many international patients consider India for this treatment due to established nuclear medicine expertise and comparatively lower costs. Eligibility and scheduling still depend on PSMA PET results, medical review, and hospital acceptance, so confirmation from the treating center is essential before planning.

items.q: Which countries offer Lu-177 PSMA therapy?
items.a: Lu-177 PSMA therapy is offered in several countries with established nuclear medicine programs, including India, Germany, the United States, China, Turkey, and others. Availability, approval status, and pricing differ between countries and individual hospitals. Some centers offer it as an approved treatment, while others provide it within specific protocols. International patients should confirm current availability, cost, and eligibility directly with the chosen center, since regulations and access can change over time.

items.q: Can Lu-177 PSMA therapy be repeated or combined with other treatments?
items.a: In some cases, Lu-177 PSMA therapy may be repeated or used alongside other treatments, depending on how the cancer responds and the patient's condition. Doctors may combine or sequence it with hormonal therapy, chemotherapy, or other approaches as part of an overall plan. Whether repetition or combination is suitable depends on PSMA expression, prior response, side effects, and organ function. These decisions are made by the treating oncology team after careful assessment.

items.q: Are there clinical trials for Lu-177 PSMA therapy?
items.a: Yes, clinical trials continue to study Lu-177 PSMA therapy in earlier disease stages, new combinations, and different patient groups. Trials may offer access to emerging approaches, but they do not guarantee enrollment or benefit. Eligibility is decided after medical record review and investigator assessment, and trials often have strict inclusion and exclusion criteria. Patients interested in trials should discuss suitable options with their oncology team and the trial center.

items.q: What newer PSMA-targeted therapies are being developed?
items.a: Researchers are developing newer PSMA-targeted therapies, including different radioactive isotopes such as Actinium-225 and improved targeting molecules. These aim to enhance effectiveness or reduce side effects for advanced prostate cancer. Many of these options remain experimental and are available mainly through clinical trials or specialized centers. Availability, evidence, and safety vary, so any newer therapy should be considered only after detailed discussion with a qualified oncology and nuclear medicine team.

items.q: What medical reports are needed for Lu-177 PSMA therapy?
items.a: Key reports for Lu-177 PSMA therapy usually include a recent PSMA PET scan, biopsy or pathology results, PSA levels, and details of previous treatments. Blood tests showing kidney function and blood counts, along with imaging such as CT or bone scans, are also important. These help specialists confirm PSMA-positive disease and assess suitability. Gathering complete and up-to-date records helps the treating center review eligibility and plan care more accurately.

items.q: How can international patients access Lu-177 PSMA therapy?
items.a: International patients can access Lu-177 PSMA therapy by sharing medical reports with a suitable center, obtaining a treatment opinion, and arranging travel if accepted. Access depends on hospital acceptance, PSMA PET confirmation, medical review, visa approval, and fitness to travel. None of these can be guaranteed in advance. Planning should also cover estimated cost, scheduling of cycles, accommodation, and follow-up care, ideally coordinated well before the intended treatment date.

items.q: What should international patients plan for during treatment abroad?
items.a: International patients should plan for the full treatment course, which may involve several cycles spaced weeks apart, plus recovery and monitoring time. Practical considerations include estimated cost, travel and visa arrangements, accommodation near the hospital, radiation safety guidance, and follow-up care after returning home. Because schedules can change based on response and blood tests, some flexibility is wise. A clear plan and a second opinion can help patients make informed, confident decisions.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with Lu-177 PSMA therapy?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organize medical reports, identify relevant specialists or treatment centers, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, travel, visa, and follow-up support for Lu-177 PSMA therapy. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified oncology team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, stage, biomarkers such as PSMA expression, previous treatment, and overall health. This support is intended to guide the process, not to replace doctors or hospitals.
